findings.claim: Three Cambridge graduates started it in 1999 with £500 of fruit. They grew via small business loans and, years later, crowdfunded rounds and a share sale to Coca-Cola. Early on they had no trading history — a bank would not lend them six-figure sums, so they relied on a mix of owner’s savings and family support.
findings.truth: Innocent's funding history is invented. The £500 of fruit and the London music-festival stall were 1998, not 1999. There were no crowdfunded rounds and no early small business loans, and the founders did not rely on family support: they struggled to raise money until the American investor Maurice Pinto put in £250,000 for a stake. Coca-Cola bought a minority stake (about 18%) for £30 million in April 2009, raised it to 58% in April 2010 and to over 90% in February 2013. The error also teaches the wrong finance lesson: the rescue was equity from an outside investor, not debt.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Innocent Drinks' (founding, Maurice Pinto £250,000, Coca-Cola stakes 2009/2010/2013)

findings.claim: Innocent Smoothies started with savings, grew via loans, then used share issues.
findings.truth: Same fabrication as F1 in the takeaway. Innocent did not grow via loans; the growth finance was an equity stake sold to a private investor, then stakes sold to Coca-Cola.

findings.claim: The AQA specification requires seven main sources. / collapsible heading 'Seven External Sources'
findings.truth: Eight external sources are then listed: family and friends, new share issue, bank loan, mortgage, overdraft, trade credit, hire purchase and government grants. The spec groups 'obtaining a loan or mortgage' as one item, which is where 'seven' comes from, but the lesson splits them. A student revising to a stated count of seven will think one of the eight is not examinable.
findings.evidence: spec 3.6.1 (specs/aqa/business-8132-8132.md lines 1551-1573); count of the lesson's own bullets

findings.claim: For 3-mark ‘Calculate’ questions, always show the working ... The method mark is half the total.
findings.truth: One method mark out of three is a third, not a half. This is an invented mark-scheme split. The true and useful point is that correct working still earns marks when the final figure is wrong.
findings.evidence: arithmetic; no such statement in the spec's assessment section (2.2, 4.2)

findings.claim: Dunelm, the UK homeware chain, sees its heaviest sales in spring/summer and has to manage tighter cash in quieter months. / sales peak in spring/summer when people refresh their homes, then dip through autumn
findings.truth: The stated direction looks reversed. Dunelm's financial year ends in late June (confirmed on its own corporate reports page), and its Christmas quarter is generally reported as its strongest trading period, which would put the peak in autumn/winter, not spring/summer. I could not open a Dunelm trading statement to read the quarterly split, so the true pattern is unconfirmed. Options: (a) check one Dunelm quarterly trading statement and reverse the direction; (b) drop the direction and keep the general point that a seasonal retailer plans supplier terms and stock around its own pattern; (c) leave it if a source confirms a spring/summer peak. The claim appears twice in content_html and once in the practice question 6 model answer.
findings.evidence: corporate.dunelm.com results and reports page (year end late June); no quarterly split obtainable
findings.ruling: Seasonal direction dropped (Dunelm's strongest quarter is Oct-Dec); the seasonality point is kept.

findings.claim: Always add the correct unit (£ or %) to the final answer — a bare number loses a mark.
findings.truth: An invented mark-scheme rule. The advice to add the unit is sound; the claim that a bare number costs a mark is not something the spec or any published rule states.
findings.evidence: spec assessment section 2.2 / 4.2; no such rule

findings.claim: AQA will not give you the formulae for break-even or ARR — memorise them. For break-even questions, always calculate contribution per unit first, then divide fixed costs by that figure.
findings.truth: Wrong exam claim. The spec states plainly that students will not be expected to draw break-even charts or use the break-even formula; they identify the break-even level of output and the margin of safety from a chart. Break-even is also absent from the quantitative-skills list, which does include average rate of return, gross and net profit margin, percentages and cash flow. The tip sends revision at a calculation that will not be asked and away from chart reading, which will.
findings.evidence: spec 3.6.3 additional information ('Students will not be expected to draw break-even charts or use the break-even formula', lines 1659-1660) and 6.1 Calculation (lines 2010-2019)

findings.claim: AQA requires interpretation of break-even charts, not drawing them from scratch. But the underlying numbers come from two formulae.
findings.truth: Half right. The spec rules out both drawing the chart and using the break-even formula. As written, the sentence leaves a student expecting to have to use the formula under exam conditions.

findings.claim: Every unit sold above the break-even point is pure profit.
findings.truth: A misconception stated as fact. Above break-even each extra unit adds its contribution, not its selling price. In the lesson's own example the 501st latte adds £2.40 of profit, not £3.50. The variable cost is still paid on every unit sold.
findings.evidence: recomputation from the lesson's figures (price £3.50, variable cost £1.10, contribution £2.40)

findings.claim: Every unit sold above this point is pure profit; every unit below is loss.
findings.truth: The same misconception in the takeaway. Each unit above break-even adds its contribution to profit.

findings.claim: Add the % sign — forgetting it loses a mark.
findings.truth: An invented mark-scheme rule, as in F6. Adding the % sign is good practice, but the penalty claim is not in the spec.
findings.evidence: spec assessment section 2.2 / 4.2; no such rule

findings.claim: [3] 'A bakery sells loaves for £2.50 each. Variable cost per loaf is £0.90. Weekly fixed costs are £800. Calculate the break-even point in units.' typed '3 marks — Calculate'
findings.truth: The arithmetic is right (£2.50 − £0.90 = £1.60; £800 ÷ £1.60 = 500 loaves), but the spec says students will not be expected to use the break-even formula, and break-even is not in the quantitative-skills list, so AQA will not set this as an exam calculation. Options: (a) keep the item but retype it as skills practice rather than an exam-tariff question; (b) replace it with a chart-reading item once a break-even chart asset exists; (c) leave it. My recommendation is (a): the working genuinely explains why the chart moves when costs or prices change, so it is worth keeping, but it should not be presented as a real exam question. The same scope note applies to knowledge check 1 and to the key-fact revision tip that asks the student to write the break-even formula from memory.
findings.ruling: NOTE: break-even formula calculation is off-spec for AQA 8132 (chart-reading only); retyping belongs to the question-type relabel sweep, recorded in corpus_notes.

findings.claim: A 30% ARR comfortably beats bank savings (around 4-5% currently).
findings.truth: Roughly right today, but 'currently' dates the lesson and the figure will go stale without anyone noticing. Worth rewording to a date-stamped or non-numeric comparison the next time this lesson is touched.
findings.evidence: no correction made; flagged for staleness only

findings.claim: Supermarkets typically run net margins of 2-5%. Luxury brands like Burberry run 15-20%.
findings.truth: Burberry's net margin is nowhere near 15-20%. In the financial year ended 28 March 2026 Burberry made £20 million of net income on £2,420 million of revenue, a net margin of about 0.8%, with operating income of £115 million. The supermarket figure is fine. The Burberry figure also undercuts the lesson's own teaching point, because it is the gross margin that is high in luxury, not necessarily the net margin.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Burberry' (FY ended 28 March 2026: revenue £2,420m, operating income £115m, net income £20m)

summary: Every number in the unit recomputes correctly: all five cash-flow, cost, break-even, margin-of-safety, ARR and profit-margin worked examples, all six calculation mark schemes, all 25 knowledge-check keys and all five match sets. Every practice tariff (1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 12) is a real AQA tariff, no lesson names a paper or section, and no SPaG claim appears. The damage is a fabricated Innocent Smoothies funding history, three invented mark-scheme rules, a scope error that tells students to memorise the break-even formula when the spec says they will not have to use it, 'every unit above break-even is pure profit' stated twice, a stale Burberry margin, and a Dunelm seasonality claim that looks reversed.
